title: Telehealth and Autism Prior to and in the Age of COVID-19: A Systematic and Critical Review of the Last Decade
venue: Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review
extended_summary:
This paper examines the evidence base for telehealth use in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) assessment and intervention over the prior decade, with added emphasis on developments accelerated by COVID-19. The review was motivated by the growing need for remote service delivery and by the limited synthesis available on telehealth applications for children and adolescents with ASD and their families.

The authors conducted a systematic search across multiple databases using PRISMA procedures, screened 472 records, and retained 55 studies after quality review. The included studies covered a range of telehealth-supported services, including diagnostic assessment, speech and language assessment, functional assessment, preference assessments, parent training, applied behavior analysis, functional communication training, and cognitive-behavioral interventions. Telehealth was delivered primarily via video conferencing, with some studies using web platforms or apps, and participants included children with ASD, parents, teachers/staff, and other interventionists.

Across studies, telehealth was generally found to be feasible, acceptable, and often comparable to in-person delivery, with many studies reporting improved fidelity, reduced problem behavior, or gains in communication and other child outcomes. The review concludes that telehealth is a promising service modality for ASD, while noting the need for continued research on feasibility, efficacy, and the digital divide that may limit access for some families.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic and critical review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not present a single pooled estimate or a controlled primary study. Its conclusions depend on heterogeneous underlying studies with varying designs and quality.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests telehealth can improve access and service delivery for ASD, but the paper itself reports no pooled medium/large effect size. The impact is therefore important but evidence is qualitative and heterogeneous rather than directly quantified.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic and critical review synthesized 55 telehealth studies in ASD and concluded that telehealth services were generally equivalent or better than face-to-face delivery across assessment and intervention contexts. The paper emphasizes implementation feasibility, access, and acceptability rather than a single effect estimate; it also notes the digital divide as an important limiting factor.
finding.measure: Systematic review of telehealth assessment/intervention outcomes, feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and diagnostic agreement across 55 studies
